body:
I enjoyed the idea behind this and the cast were great. I especially liked Halle Berry's character, all too true for older women in the workplace. I hope the insurance company suffered from that final diamond heist - how ironic that would have been.

But, like so many movies today, it was just tooo long, so you had filler characters that appeared then disappeared. The main characters should have had more screen time, it would have resulted in a tighter plot too.

Still, I don't usually like heist movies but this was pretty OK.

Crime 101 left me with genuinely mixed emotions. The cast is one of the film's strongest assets - Chris Hemsworth, Halle Berry, and Mark Ruffalo all deliver committed performances, and you can feel their effort in every scene. The core idea of the story is intriguing, and there's real potential in its themes and character dynamics. Visually, the film has quality; some moments are shot beautifully and carry a strong cinematic presence.

However, the biggest weakness for me lies in the writing and direction. The tension-building sequences feel overstretched and forced, and instead of creating suspense, they become exhausting. I often felt tired rather than invested during crucial moments. The protagonist's character arc is also uneven - he starts as a disciplined, rule-driven man, but his shift in behavior feels unearned and poorly developed.

Overall, Crime 101 isn't a bad film, but its inconsistent writing and dragged pacing hold it back from becoming the gripping crime drama it could have been.

Ultimately, Crime 101 is a cerebral crime drama that prioritizes mood, character, and thematic depth over spectacle. It's a film that invites viewers to think rather than simply watch, offering a nuanced exploration of obsession and identity. While it may not satisfy those seeking adrenaline-fueled entertainment, it stands out as a sophisticated and haunting addition to the crime genre.

Strong performances, nice secondary characters enrich rather than messify with some nice tense scenes and well executed action.

Not quite up there with a Michael Mann or David Fincher, but good enough to while away a couple of hours... Just think, though; they DID aim high with this one, getting Hemsworth as a lead, whereas were it not so ambitious, they'd've got one of the Amells - who would've been terrific; it's just that Hemsworth adds that little extra zip.

Rarely has a film convinced me for so long only to let me down at the very last moment. Bart Layton builds a Los Angeles noir with a dense, carefully controlled texture - balancing rhythm and depth with a precision rarely seen in contemporary cinema.

One hundred and forty minutes that never drag, carried by a cast that gives you no excuse to look away.

Chris Hemsworth surprises with restraint: his Davis is a character built by subtraction, where silence carries as much weight as action.

Mark Ruffalo is the perfect counterbalance - a detective more Columbo than cowboy, tenacious and almost endearingly stubborn.

Halle Berry completes a well-calibrated narrative triangle in which no one is entirely a hero and no one entirely a villain.

Then the ending arrives. And something breaks.

After so much care, the closing feels rushed, almost improvised - as if the screenplay had run out of ideas at the precise moment it needed its decisive move. A tremendous shame, because up until then the film deserved a far more generous score.

What remains is a solid, mature, recommendable work - but with the bitter aftertaste of something that came close to greatness without ever quite reaching it.
